outcomes.original: Filing step: Form the California legal entity (LLC or corporation) with the Secretary of State and obtain a federal Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. What to say: File Articles of Organization (LLC-1, $70) or Articles of Incorporation (ARTS-GS, $100) on the California Secretary of State bizfile Online portal. The entity name must match the lease and the CUA application. Within 90 days file the Statement of Information ($20 LLC, due every two years; $25 corporation, due annually). Once the entity is approved, apply for an EIN online at irs.gov; it is issued immediately and free. The EIN is required before opening a business bank account, registering for payroll taxes, and filing the San Francisco Business Registration Certificate.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Register the business with the San Francisco Treasurer & Tax Collector to obtain a Business Account Number (BAN), and file a Fictitious Business Name (DBA) statement with the County Clerk if the public-facing name differs from the legal entity name. What to say: Apply online for a San Francisco Business Registration Certificate; the fee is tiered by gross receipts (e.g. $55 for under $100k, $95 for $100k–$250k, plus a $4 state fee). The BAN is issued within 1–5 days and is required for every other city permit and license. If operating as 'Super Duper Burgers' under an entity with a different legal name, file the Fictitious Business Name statement with the SF County Clerk ($60–120), then publish the statement in a court-approved newspaper once a week for four weeks and file proof of publication within 45 days. Banks and the building permit application require the filed DBA statement.

outcomes.original: Filing step: Once the CUA is approved by the Planning Commission, wait out the 30-day appeal period, then file the building permit application with DBI and proceed with tenant improvement construction. What to say: After the Planning Commission approves the CUA by Motion, the decision is not final until the 30-day appeal period expires (or any appeal is resolved). Once final, submit the building permit application to DBI with the approved CUA Motion number, stamped architectural plans, MEP plans signed by licensed contractors, and proof of workers' compensation insurance. Pay the building permit fee (calculated as a percentage of construction valuation, typically $800–$15,000 for a restaurant TI). DBI will route the application to Planning, DPH, SFFD, SFPUC, and other departments as needed. Address any plan check corrections promptly. Schedule inspections (rough, final, hood suppression, fire, health pre-opening) at each construction milestone. Do not open to the public until the final DBI sign-off, the SFFD inspection, and the DPH health permit to operate are issued.

outcomes.original: Estimated time: 120 to 300 days. Estimated government cost: $5,800 to $22,000. Notes: This is a timeline and cost range for the approvals in the entitlement path when they are granted: Conditional Use Authorization and Health permit to operate. The CUA in NCT-FILLMORE typically takes 120–300 days from filing to Planning Commission approval, including pre-application meeting, environmental review, 300-foot mailed notice, and hearing scheduling. The comparable formula retail CUAs took 167 days (Pinot's Palette, 2015-007413CUA) and 364 days (Orangetheory Fitness, 2018-009861CUA); the cancelled Super Duper CUA at this address took 517 days before cancellation, but that is not a time to approval. Health permit plan check and issuance after final inspection adds 21–60 days for plan review plus 14–45 days for permit issuance, typically overlapping with CUA review and construction. Total government costs: CUA application fee approximately $3,100 (2025–26 schedule for formula retail), DPH plan check $2,207, health permit application $470, business registration $55–700, and building permit $800–15,000 (varies by construction valuation). This does not include construction costs, architect fees, or the building permit timeline (14–120 days for plan check and inspections). The day range is from CUA filing to Commission approval and health permit issuance; it does not include the 30-day appeal period after CUA approval or the time to complete tenant improvement construction.
